item.title: China strengthens protection for growing snow leopard population
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-24
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's snow leopard population has doubled to about 5,000 from around 2,500 in 2013, reflecting progress in protecting the species and its habitat. The latest figures were released by the National Forestry and Grassland Administration on Friday on the occasion of the International Day of the Snow Leopard which falls on Oct. 23. Snow leopards typically inhabit rugged terrain at elevations of 3,000 to 5,000 meters and serve as an important indicator of the health of high-altitude mountain ecosystems. The species is classified as "vulnerable" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List of Threatened Species and receives the highest level of wildlife protection in China. China has the world's largest snow leopard population and protects more than 60 percent of the species' global habitat, according to the administration. Its habitat covers about 2.08 million square kilometers across eight provincial-level regions. China has taken a systematic approach to snow leopard conservation since 2013. Its protection network includes two national parks and 78 other important protected areas in key snow leopard habitats. More than 800,000 square kilometers of habitat are under strict protection, while nearly 40 percent of the species' potential habitat is under standardized management. The country is also using technologies such as infrared cameras and DNA analysis of fecal samples to monitor snow leopard populations, track their movements and study their breeding activity. Sustained conservation efforts have improved snow leopard habitat quality and ecosystem integrity, alongside growth in the population and its reproductive vitality, the administration said. In April, infrared cameras in the Helan Mountains in northwest China captured a reintroduced female snow leopard with her cub, marking the first time a snow leopard reintroduction project worldwide has resulted in cubs being born and successfully raised in the wild. Native to the Helan Mountains, snow leopards disappeared from the area in the 1950s due to habitat destruction and human disturbance. To restore the population, eight snow leopards have been introduced to the mountains so far. Several snow leopards, including those arriving naturally, have since established territories and hunt independently. Signs of the species' presence are also emerging elsewhere. In Muli County of Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Sichuan Province, footage recorded this year confirmed the first sighting of a snow leopard in the prefecture, extending the known southeastern edge of the species' range, the administration said. Looking ahead, China will focus on improving connectivity between habitats, protecting genetic diversity and refining measures to prevent and address human-wildlife conflict to sustain snow leopard population recovery, the administration said. ■

item.title: FAO honors highlight China's efforts to strengthen global food security
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
* The recent FAO honors awarded to Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen and a Chinese research institute highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation. * Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action. * Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems. * In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management. ROME, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- As Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen was honored at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome, her longtime American friend Ronald Sakolsky looked on, his eyes filled with tears. "Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," said Sakolsky, a retired teacher who helped fund her tree-planting efforts more than two decades ago. At the Oct. 15 ceremony, Yin was named among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, an initiative marking the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026. A day later, a Chinese research institute received an FAO award for its crop-monitoring technology. Together, the honors highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation. FROM SHIFTING SANDS TO A GREEN LANDSCAPE The story of Yin and Sakolsky began in 1999, when Sakolsky was teaching in central China's Henan Province. After seeing a TV report about Yin's efforts to hold back the encroaching sands in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, he raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her afforestation endeavor. After losing touch for years, the two reunited in Inner Mongolia in August 2026. By then, the seedlings supported by Sakolsky's donation had grown into more than 50,000 trees. Since planting her first tree in 1986, Yin has helped green over 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) of sandy land, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Today, the area supports a greater variety of crops and plants, including cherries and roses, creating new opportunities for agricultural production and income growth. "I have spent more than 40 years transforming this desert, and now all kinds of food can grow here," Yin told Xinhua. Yin's efforts reflect China's broader push to combat desertification, a major part of which is the Three-North Shelterbelt Forest Program, launched in 1978 to restore degraded land and strengthen ecological security in northern China. For Yin, combating desertification is also essential to agricultural production. "If we cannot control the sand, how can we grow good crops when sandstorms come? How can we improve the soil?" she said. At the World Food Day ceremony in Rome on Oct. 16, Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action. "It must be the steady kind that plants, tends and finally harvests the gains. As did Yin Yuzhen," the princess said. INNOVATION FOR GLOBAL FOOD SECURITY Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems. On Oct. 16, the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences received the 2026 FAO Achievement Award for its CropWatch, a cloud-based crop-monitoring platform. Developed by a team led by researcher Wu Bingfang, the platform combines satellite observations with climate and agricultural data to monitor crop conditions, assess production prospects and identify risks such as drought and abnormal rainfall. Through its open cloud service, CropWatch allows users to conduct their own crop assessments without investing heavily in local computing infrastructure. According to the research team, the platform has helped more than 40 countries and regions monitor crop conditions, and its bulletins have served users in 173 countries and regions. CropWatch has also been integrated into the FAO's Hand-in-Hand Geospatial Platform and the Group on Earth Observations Knowledge Hub. It serves as an important channel and an independent source of timely crop monitoring information for users worldwide. Wu told Xinhua after receiving the award that the recognition affirmed the team's more than three decades of dedication. "This is not the end, but a milestone on a new journey ahead," he said. SHARING CHINESE EXPERIENCE FOR FOOD SECURITY China's contribution extends beyond domestic production to international agricultural cooperation. In addition to feeding its own population of more than 1.4 billion, China has also provided assistance to countries in need, contributing to global food security. Zhang Lubiao, China's permanent representative to the FAO, said China would deepen cooperation with the FAO in hybrid rice, water-saving irrigation, digital agriculture and climate-adaptive technologies, among other areas. Such cooperation is already yielding tangible results in various countries. Nosipho Jezile, South Africa's permanent representative to the UN food and agriculture agencies, said China's South-South cooperation projects with the FAO had supported rice cultivation, aquaculture, irrigation infrastructure, mechanization and agricultural innovation in African countries. "These projects have brought tangible increases in output and created employment opportunities," she said. Food security depends on more than agricultural production. Keeping food affordable and ensuring a stable supply of fertilizers and other agricultural inputs are also essential, particularly amid economic and geopolitical uncertainties. In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said rising prices, rather than immediate food shortages, posed the biggest risk to global food security at present. Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management. China's urea exports were also helping bring down prices, he said, urging major producers and importers not to distort markets or restrict exports of agricultural inputs. ■

item.title: Xiplomacy: Reading Xi's vision for global governance through metaphors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) is set to open on Friday in the Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province, bringing into world focus a pressing question: How can countries work together to address shared challenges in an interconnected world amid growing protectionism and unilateralism? In speeches and meetings on multiple occasions, Chinese President Xi Jinping has used vivid metaphors to articulate his vision for global governance. These metaphors offer insights into his approach to building a more just, equitable and inclusive global governance system. IN SAME BOAT "I was looking at the vast ocean when I boarded the ship, and it struck me that we are all indeed fellow passengers in the same boat," Xi said while addressing the 2018 APEC CEO Summit hosted at a unique setting -- onboard the giant cruise Pacific Explorer in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea. The metaphor embodies the essence of Xi's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, highlighting the interconnectedness of countries and the need for solidarity and cooperation in addressing common challenges. Today, the interconnected world is grappling with four mounting deficits: a peace deficit that exacerbates geopolitical conflicts, a development deficit that widens the North-South divide, a security deficit that erodes mutual trust, and a governance deficit that undermines the effectiveness of multilateralism. In 2019, at the China-France Global Governance Forum held in Paris, Xi proposed a four-pronged approach to addressing the four deficits. First and foremost, he called for fairness and reasonableness to address the governance deficit. "It is advisable to uphold a vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefits," Xi said, calling for actively advancing the democratization of global governance rules. As the world has found itself in a new period of turbulence and transformation, global governance has come to a new crossroads. Against this backdrop, Xi put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in September 2025 in China's coastal city of Tianjin. "I look forward to working with all countries for a more just and equitable global governance system and advancing toward a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said, stressing sovereign equality and genuine multilateralism. TRAFFIC LIGHTS "A world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed," Xi said at the 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India. This metaphor highlights the importance of rules in maintaining the international order. While having rules in place matters, how they are made and who gets to make them matter even more. International rules must be written and upheld jointly by all countries based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, rather than dictated by those with the strongest muscles or the loudest voice, Xi once stressed. He has also called for the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations to be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety. "There should be no double standards, and the house rules of a few countries must not be imposed upon others," he said. The GGI proposed by President Xi reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a fairer and more representative system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University. MAKING THE PIE BIGGER Xi has repeatedly used the metaphor of a pie to describe the gains of international cooperation. "We should make the pie of win-win cooperation bigger, and ensure that more development gains will be shared more fairly by people across the world," he said at the 23rd meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in 2023. The pie metaphor reflects the people-centered and action-oriented vision of the GGI: making the gains of cooperation bigger while ensuring that they are shared more widely and fairly. When proposing the GGI, Xi emphasized the importance of "ensuring that the people of every nation are the actors in and beneficiaries of global governance." The SCO, the platform where Xi proposed the GGI, provides an example. Within the grouping, China has announced the establishment of cooperation platforms in energy, green industries and the digital economy, as well as centers for scientific and technological innovation, higher education, and vocational and technical education. The expanding scope of cooperation shows how the "pie" can be made bigger in practice: by opening up new areas of cooperation, creating more opportunities for development and ensuring that the benefits reach more people. Beyond making the pie bigger, Xi has also called for sharing the pie fairly to ensure justice and equity. For him, the ultimate purpose of better global governance is to promote common development and improve people's well-being across the globe. At the G20 summit held in Brazil in 2024, Xi called for building a just world of common development, saying "prosperity and stability would not be possible in a world where the rich become richer while the poor are made poorer, and countries should make global development more inclusive, beneficial to all, and more resilient." To build such a world, Xi said, there should be more bridges of cooperation, and less "small yard, high fences," so that more and more developing countries will be better off and achieve modernization. ■

item.title: China issues guidelines to promote employment amid AI advances
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has rolled out guidelines on adapting to advances in artificial intelligence (AI) to promote employment-friendly development, aiming to harness the technology to create jobs, improve employment quality and stimulate entrepreneurship while mitigating job displacement caused by AI applications. The guidelines, issued by the General Office of the State Council, set out 18 tasks in six areas, including boosting AI's job-creation potential, making AI adoption more employment-friendly, improving workers' digital skills, enhancing employment services, strengthening labor and social security protections, and monitoring and addressing employment risks. The guidelines call for expanding employment opportunities in emerging fields, helping micro, small and medium-sized enterprises stabilize and expand employment, fostering new forms of employment and entrepreneurship in the AI sector, and developing new AI-related occupations. The guidelines urge efforts to tap AI's job-creation potential in traditional sectors, mitigate job displacement caused by AI applications, and establish a mechanism to assess employment risks associated with AI adoption. The guidelines emphasize improving the framework for protecting workers' rights in human-machine collaboration, strengthening social security for people in flexible employment and those in new forms of employment, and refining income distribution mechanisms to adapt to advances in AI. The guidelines outline coordinated efforts to cultivate innovative AI talent and implement specialized AI training programs. They also propose using AI to support the implementation of employment policies and make employment services more intelligent, while increasing support for workers transitioning to new jobs. Further measures include strengthening monitoring and early warning of employment risks associated with AI applications, deepening research into their impact on employment, and improving mechanisms for responding to such risks. The guidelines come as AI adoption expands across China's economy. The country's core AI industry was valued at more than 1.2 trillion yuan (about 178.62 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with more than 6,200 AI companies operating nationwide, according to official figures. By the end of 2025, more than 30 percent of manufacturing enterprises with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan had adopted AI technologies. A five-year plan for the employment-first strategy highlights promoting employment alongside AI advancements as a key task. It calls for creating new jobs through AI applications and unlocking employment potential in traditional industries. AI is already reshaping China's economy and transforming its labor market, with demand growing for workers equipped with specialized technical skills. According to Maimai, a networking and recruitment platform, the number of new AI-related job postings in the new economy on the platform rose 789.47 percent year on year from January to July. Online job-seeking platform Zhaopin also reported particularly strong demand for AI engineers, including those working in automotive manufacturing and intelligent driving. ■

item.title: Xi orders all-out rescue efforts after 7.0-magnitude earthquake in Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has ordered all-out search and rescue efforts for the missing and prompt medical treatment for the injured after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck a county in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Thursday night. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, urged in an important instruction every effort to minimize casualties. The earthquake struck Baqen County in Nagqu City, Xizang, at 10:33 p.m. Thursday. The quake has left 16 people dead and 65 injured, according to local authorities. Noting that the affected area is at a high altitude with low temperatures, Xi stressed the need to closely monitor seismic activity and weather conditions to prevent secondary disasters. Efforts should be made to properly accommodate the affected residents, repair damaged infrastructure as quickly as possible, and safeguard people's lives and property, Xi said. Premier Li Qiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, called for solid disaster prevention and response efforts. The Ministry of Emergency Management and authorities in Xizang have mobilized resources for rescue and relief operations. ■

item.title: Xi chairs CPC leadership meeting to review disciplinary inspection report
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee held a meeting on Friday to review a report on the seventh round of disciplinary inspection launched by the 20th CPC Central Committee. Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, chaired the meeting. The meeting hailed the work performance and results of the inspection. According to the inspection results, central Party and government departments have made progress in their work, but some problems still exist and need to be taken seriously. The meeting urged solid efforts to rectify the problems identified by the inspection. It called on central Party and government departments to strengthen their sense of political responsibility in performing their duties, deepen reform, and ensure both development and security. It also stressed the need to strengthen leadership teams, while adopting higher standards and taking more concrete measures to advance full and rigorous Party self-governance. The meeting also discussed other matters. ■

item.title: Xi sends message to 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan)
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a message to the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) on Friday. The world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing, Xi said. "I have put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world," he said. China stands ready to work with all parties to uphold the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, pool strength through confidence-building and tackle challenges through cooperation, Xi said. He called for efforts to promote the implementation of the GGI to inject more certainty and positive energy into a world of turbulence and transformation, and jointly move toward a community with a shared future for humanity. The forum opened on the same day in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province. Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, it is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World." ■
